cells.tense: You are standing where the structure holds, and your hand is still on it.
cells.ask: Name one thing you are keeping and what it cost, then say it to someone who pays part of that cost.
cells.core:
What the change left in you got built into something with edges — hours that keep their shape, a set of things that stay where you put them — and it stands because you keep standing it up. That is not hoarding. You set it down where it can be seen.

Steadiness like this runs on give and take. You keep the parts that carry you and you hand back what you took from the people inside it. When the exchange stops, the structure turns on you and keeps you out of your own life. Name one thing you are keeping and what it cost. Then say it to someone who pays part of that price. Fair exchange keeps the shape alive, and alive is the point.
cells.sheetLine: You keep the shape, and you own the keeping.
cells.verb: holding the shape the change left behind
cells.place: at the bench, setting things in order that hold

cells.tense: You are bracing for an outcome that has not arrived, and the bracing is already rearranging the room.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you are gripping hard and leave it imperfect for a day — just watch what happens.
cells.core:
You are guarding something that isn't finished. Somewhere ahead is a version where this holds and nothing slips, and you are living there already — locking doors early, setting order before order is needed. The worry is doing its job. The timing is off. What you are protecting gets smaller under all that guarding.

Order that serves what it holds can breathe. Watch for one thing you are gripping too hard and leave it imperfect for a day. Nothing falls apart in a day. You might find the shape holds itself, or find the thing that needed protecting was not the thing you were holding. Either way you learn what the grip was for.

cells.tense: A doorway closed behind you and you have not turned around to see the room.
cells.ask: Do the smallest useful next thing in front of you — one task, ten minutes — and let direction come from the doing.
cells.core:
You are standing on the near side of a change that already happened. The order you used to keep is gone — the room emptied, the old pattern no longer fits — and you have not built anything to take its place. You see that. Seeing it is not the problem. Building is.

What brings you back is motion, not planning. Do the smallest useful thing in front of you. One task. Set the next hour in order and stop reviewing the last one. Momentum comes from the feet, not from the head. In a while the shape will be standing again and you will be inside it — not because you figured out what it should be, but because you started building.

cells.tense: You are setting the order in the room and calling it what the room already wanted.
cells.ask: Say 'I set this up' about one thing you have been calling the natural order — in your own head is enough to start.
cells.core:
You are already the one arranging the pattern — what the day looks like, who stands where, what counts as normal. The people around you are following something you made, and you have been describing it as how things simply are. It works. That is why nobody questions it. Not even you.

The making is not in question. Whether you own it is. Say it out loud — or name it to yourself — about one arrangement you have been treating as gravity. Structure that knows itself is steadiness. Structure that pretends it is nature is a load you carry without knowing it is yours. Claim the one thing and the rest gets lighter, not heavier.

attempts.check: The record shows Emotion Fruition seated in Authority, but whether what settled in this person's life is actually ready to be held — or whether the order in the room simply looks like Fruition from outside — isn't settled by anything in the draw. No cell says what changed, what ended, who was there, or how long the holding has gone on; the Too Little cell only puts a room behind them and never says what happened in it. The asks survive a wrong read: each is one visible act, doable today without money, energy, another person or spare time, and none makes the reading's truth a condition of doing it. The sentence that would serve me more than them is 'You are the one arranging the pattern, and you know it' — cut, because it tells them their own state and hands my seat-reading back as praise.
